full_judgment: 42. Vedic literature, as has been observed by Dr. Mares Chandra Sen Gupta in his Tagore Law Lectures, 1950 'Evolution of Ancient Indian Law" at page 12, has very little to say about the proprietary right of wives. She was however not incapable of acquiring properties despite a saying of Mann that woman could hold no property, but her property was naturally small, ornaments, domestic utensils and the like. In different Texts of Smriti literature, several kinds of properties which might be owned by a woman were mentioned as Stridhan, which were, mainly, gifts and presents and did not include any inherited property. Women did not figure in the scheme of inheritance yet. The preservation of the family entity appears to have been the main concern of the early exponents of law and the law of primogeniture seems to have held sway in the early stages. Subsequently ancestral property was regarded as a sort of corporate property of the agnatic descendants of the ancestor and propinquity of blood was generally the basis of the law of inheritance. But gradually a change in the legal concept took place with the change in the religio-social ideas.
